questions.prompt:
Read: "Sami has worked at the hospital for ten years. He has never taken a long holiday. This year, he has decided to travel."
Which sentence is TRUE?

options.text: Sami took a long holiday last year.
Sami has worked at the hospital for ten years.
Sami has decided not to travel.

questions.explanation: The text says "Sami has worked at the hospital for ten years", so "Sami has worked at the hospital for ten years" is true. He has never taken a long holiday ("Sami took a long holiday last year" is false), the ten years show he didn't start this year "Sami started working this year", and he has decided to travel, not to stay "Sami has decided not to travel".

options.text: I've known him since we were children.
Have you finished your work yet?
She has wrote to me twice this month.
We haven't seen them for ages.

questions.explanation: The error is "She has wrote to me twice this month": after has we need the past participle written, not the past simple wrote — She has written to me. "I've known him since we were children", "Have you finished your work yet?" and "We haven't seen them for ages" correctly use since, yet and for with the present perfect.

questions.prompt: Complete: "I can't find my phone anywhere. I think I ___ it!"
questions.explanation: The past action has a result now (the phone is missing), so we use the present perfect: I've lost it. The past simple "lost" names no time and breaks the now-link, "was losing" is continuous, and "had lost" is the past perfect.

questions.prompt: Complete: "We ___ each other since we were at university together."
questions.explanation: "since…" describes a state lasting from the past until now, so we use the present perfect: We have known each other since… "know" is the present simple, "knew" cuts the link to now, and know is a stative verb, so "are knowing" is not used.

questions.prompt: Complete the reply: "Would you like some lunch?" — "No thanks, I ___ eaten."
questions.explanation: To explain why you don't want lunch now, use the present perfect with already: I've already eaten. "didn't" is past simple without a participle, "'ve yet" is wrong (yet is for questions/negatives), and "am already" doesn't form the present perfect.

questions.prompt:
Read: "The kitchen floor is shining and still wet, and there is an empty bucket by the door. Nadia is putting the mop away."
What has Nadia probably just done?
questions.explanation: The clues — a wet, shining floor, an empty bucket and a mop being put away — show she has cleaned the floor. Cooking "She has cooked dinner", breaking a glass "She has broken a glass" and watering plants "She has watered the plants" don't fit a mop, a bucket and a wet floor.
